reading.body:
Carrie Adams is named on three AI lobbying filings, all filed through one firm for a single client, and those filings name fifteen separate bills.

The pattern is concentration on the client side and breadth on the legislative side. One client, THE AI POLICY NETWORK INC., accounts for all three filings, and one firm, uid 060dc152, is the channel for all of them. Yet the same three filings reach fifteen bills, which means a small number of disclosure documents covers a wide set of legislative targets. The disclosed prior positions run through Senate and House offices, including staff roles for Schumer, Fetterman, Pelosi, and the House Committee on Rules, which is the background the Lobbying Disclosure Act requires filers to list for the prior twenty years.

For AI specifically, this is the staffing layer of AI policy rather than the compute layer. Nothing here concerns data centers, power contracts, or interconnection. What it shows is that AI legislation is being worked by people who recently held senior staff positions in the offices that write and schedule it, and that a single client can be attached to fifteen bills at once. That is a fact about how AI policy moves through Congress, not about how AI is built.

What the data does not tell the reader is large. It does not say what was lobbied for or against on any bill, what the bills contain, whether any became law, or how much was spent. It does not establish that the prior positions and the current filings are connected beyond the disclosure requirement that puts them on the same form. It covers three filings and one lobbyist, and it draws no conclusion about her.
